title: Jericho Trumpet Deposit
subject: Contracts
stem:
Timothy, a cheerful but chronically overextended collector of Christian festival props, received an audio message from Lydia, his careful aunt, who kept a color-coded prayer-and-budget journal:

“On Reformation Day next month, I will send you $7,200 to help you get your finances steady. Spend it wisely; this is the last rescue I can make.”

Before that day, Timothy signed a contract with a festival vendor to rent a $58,000 portable “Jericho trumpet” sound-and-light rig and to make a $7,200 deposit the morning after Reformation Day. After Lydia learned of the rental contract, she repudiated her promise.

If Timothy sues Lydia for $7,200, which of the following is Lydia’s best defense?
call: Which of the following is Lydia's best defense?

choices.A: Reliance by the promisee on a promise to make a future gift does not make the promise enforceable unless that reliance also results in an economic benefit to the promisor.
choices.B: Reliance by the promisee on a promise to make a future gift does not make the promise enforceable unless injustice can be avoided only by such enforcement.
choices.C: A promise to make a gift in the future is not enforceable.
choices.D: Reliance by the promisee on a promise to make a future gift does not make the promise enforceable unless the value of the promised gift is substantially equivalent to the promisee's loss by reliance.

rightExplanation:
B is correct. The answer names the real promissory-estoppel gate: reliance on a future gift promise matters only if enforcement is needed to avoid injustice.

Gold Key: A future gift promise can be enforceable by promissory estoppel, but only through the actual reliance gates: expected reliance, actual reliance, and injustice. No “equivalent loss” gate and no “benefit to promisor” gate is part of the rule.

Silver Key: Read the array as a gate list. Three choices either delete the reliance exception or invent extra gates. B is the only choice that names the real gate.

Timothy did rely by signing the rental contract. But his reliance—renting a $58,000 Jericho-trumpet rig right after receiving a promise meant to help him get financially steady—cuts against the claim that justice requires enforcing Lydia’s promise. That makes B Lydia’s best defense.

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text: A adds an economic-benefit-to-promisor condition. That condition is not in the Gold Key gate list. NOT_TRUE → fabricated_rule.

c3.label: CUT C
c3.text: C says future gift promises are not enforceable. The absolute deletes the reliance exception. NOT_TRUE → tiered_absolute.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: D adds a substantial-equivalence requirement. That is a made-up math gate. NOT_TRUE → fabricated_rule.

c3.label: Residual B
c3.text: B states the actual gate: enforcement only if needed to avoid injustice. The stem gives Lydia a strong defense on that gate because Timothy’s reliance conflicts with the financial-stability purpose of the promised gift.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: Not reached after CUT. One answer survives.

studentScript: Gift promise plus reliance. Real gate is injustice. The rental reliance undercuts justice. B.

A.signal: The choice adds a condition not in the Gold Key gate list.
A.lawyer: Promissory estoppel does not require economic benefit to the promisor; Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 90 focuses on expected reliance, actual reliance, and injustice.

B.signal: This choice names the real gate and answers Lydia's defense.
B.lawyer: This tracks Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 90 and applies the injustice requirement to Timothy's inconsistent reliance.

C.signal: The absolute deletes the reliance exception taught by the Gold Key.
C.lawyer: A gratuitous promise may be enforceable under promissory estoppel when § 90 is satisfied; this statement is overbroad.

D.signal: The choice turns the injustice standard into a made-up math match.
D.lawyer: Restatement § 90 does not require the promised gift to equal the reliance loss; the remedy may be limited as justice requires.

goldKeys.statement: A future gift promise can be enforceable by promissory estoppel only when the promisor should expect reliance, reliance occurs, and enforcement is needed to avoid injustice; the rule does not require equivalent loss or a benefit to the promisor.
goldKeys.trigger: a gratuitous future promise followed by reliance and a defense asking why enforcement should fail
goldKeys.unlocks: the future-gift-is-never-enforceable trap and the two invented extra-gate traps

silverKeys.statement: When every choice says future gift plus reliance unless something else, read the answers as a gate list. Keep the choice that names the real gate, then use the stem facts to see whether that gate helps the defending party.
silverKeys.trigger: one choice deletes the reliance exception, two choices invent extra conditions, and one choice names the injustice gate

remediation.title: Promissory Estoppel Gate List
remediation.studentMove: When reliance appears after a future gift promise, cut broad no-gift and invented-extra-gate answers.
remediation.tinyRule: Gift promise plus reliance can be enforceable only if enforcement is needed to avoid injustice.
